titleText.es: La batería de un portátil contiene más o menos la energía de una granada de mano, y si la cortocircuitas... ¡Oye! ¡No puedes arrestarme solo por demostrar que vuestras leyes son inconsistentes!
titleText.en: A laptop battery contains roughly the stored energy of a hand grenade, and if shorted it ... hey!  You can't arrest me if I prove your rules inconsistent!
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive; the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute, including its spacing and ellipsis style.

regions.labelEs: PERO SI ESTÁIS PREOCUPADOS POR LAS BOMBAS, ¿POR QUÉ ME DEJÁIS METER LA BATERÍA DEL PORTÁTIL? SI LA SOMETO A SOBREVOLTAJE Y ROMPO LAS CELDAS, PROVOCARÍA UNA EXPLOSIÓN CONSIDERABLE.

applications.explanationEn: Estáis matches the people addressed, preocupados describes that plural group, and por introduces las bombas as the source of concern.
The -áis ending marks the several people addressed informally in the vosotros form used mainly in Spain.
The two-word accented form por qué introduces this direct question asking for a reason.
Me identifies the person receiving permission, dejáis matches the people allowing it, and meter stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the allowed action.
The -áis ending marks the several people addressed informally in the vosotros form used mainly in Spain.
La replaces the affected battery, someto is the speaker's form of someter, and a introduces sobrevoltaje as the applied condition.
Provocaría keeps the full verb provocar and adds -ía to present the explosion as a conditional result.
Considerable follows explosión in the common neutral order for a description.
Considerable is singular to match singular explosión and has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

regions.labelEs: NO PASA NADA, QUERIDA. EN SEGUIDA SE DARÁ CUENTA DE QUE TENGO RAZÓN Y ME DEVOLVERÁ EL AGUA.

applications.explanationEn: The complete fixed expression reassures the listener that the alarming situation is not a problem.
En seguida places the expected realization in the immediate future.
Se matches the person expected to realize something, dará supplies the future form of dar, cuenta completes the expression, and de que opens the fact to be recognized.
Dará keeps the dictionary form dar and adds -á for a future action by one other person or thing.
Tengo matches the speaker, and razón completes the conventional expression for claiming to be right.
Devolverá keeps the dictionary form devolver and adds -á for a future action by one other person or thing.
Agua remains feminine, but its initial stressed a sound makes singular el the article used immediately before it.

cards.answerEn: you all are (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Estáis is the present form of estar used with vosotros or vosotras when speaking informally to several people, mainly in Spain.

example.en: You all are at home.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is worried about something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar, the matching form of preocupado, then por and the cause.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time. Preocupado changes its ending to match whom it describes: preocupado, preocupada, preocupados, or preocupadas. Por remains unchanged before the source of concern.

example.es: Lucía está preocupada por su perro.
example.en: Lucía is worried about her dog.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.noteEn: Preocupados describes more than one masculine person or a mixed group. A feminine group uses preocupadas.

example.es: Mis vecinos están preocupados por el humo.
example.en: My neighbors are worried about the smoke.

cards.answerEn: about; required after preocupado before the cause of concern
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses por after preocupado, preocupada, preocupados, or preocupadas to introduce what causes the worry.

example.en: We are worried about the exam.

cards.noteEn: Bomba can also mean a pump. Here the plural refers specifically to explosive devices.

example.es: Los artificieros retiraron dos bombas antiguas.
example.en: The bomb squad removed two old bombs.

cards.noteEn: Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.answerEn: me (the speaker as the person allowed to act)
cards.noteEn: In a request such as deja que me siente, me belongs with the following action and identifies the speaker. Natural English likewise uses “me” after “let.”

example.en: Let me sit here.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone lets another person do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, mark the person receiving permission with me, te, le, nos, os, or les, and put the allowed action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form is the verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The person marker can stand before a changed form of dejar, join an affirmative command such as déjame, or in some structures join the following dictionary-form verb. Dejar changes for the person and time; the allowed action does not.

example.en: My mother lets me drive.

cards.answerEn: you all let; you all allow (informal, mainly Spain)
cards.noteEn: Dejáis is the present form of dejar used with vosotros or vosotras. In this use, the person being allowed acts next.

example.en: Are you all letting the children enter?

cards.noteEn: Meter describes placing something inside a container, space, or situation.

example.es: Mete la carta en el sobre.
example.en: Put the letter in the envelope.

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.noteEn: As a noun in computing, el portátil is a laptop. As an adjective, portátil means portable.

example.es: Mi portátil necesita una batería nueva.
example.en: My laptop needs a new battery.

cards.promptEs: someter algo a + prueba o condición
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is subjected to a test, force, or condition?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of someter, name or replace the affected thing, then use a before the test or condition.
cards.noteEn: Someter changes for the person and time. The affected thing can be named with a noun or replaced by a short word such as lo or la. The preposition a stays unchanged before what is applied to it.

example.es: Sometieron la tela a mucho calor.
example.en: They subjected the fabric to intense heat.

cards.answerEn: I subject; I expose (something to a condition)
cards.noteEn: Someto is the present form of someter used with yo. The thing affected normally comes before a, and the test or condition comes after a.

example.en: I subject the sample to pressure.

cards.answerEn: to; required after someter before the condition
cards.noteEn: In someter algo a una prueba o condición, a introduces the test, force, or condition applied to the affected thing.

example.es: Sometieron el motor a varias pruebas.
example.en: They subjected the engine to several tests.

cards.noteEn: Rompo is the irregular present form of romper used with yo.

example.en: I break the seal carefully.

cards.noteEn: In a battery, a celda is one electrochemical unit. The same word can mean other kinds of enclosed cells in different contexts.

example.en: The battery contains six cells.

cards.noteEn: Provocaría keeps the full verb provocar and adds -ía to describe a conditional result.

example.en: An error would cause another delay.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

example.en: We would travel by train.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Here considerable describes something notably large rather than merely worthy of consideration.

example.es: El arreglo requiere una cantidad considerable.
example.en: The repair requires a substantial amount.

cards.answerEn: oh; an exclamation of alarm or annoyance

cards.noteEn: Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’

example.en: Man, it's been so long!

cards.questionEn: How can you reassure someone that there is no problem or that something is okay?
cards.noteEn: The expression literally uses pasar and nada, but it conventionally reassures someone that nothing bad is happening or that a mistake does not matter.

example.en: —Sorry for arriving late. —No problem.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

example.en: I don’t see anything.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en seguida, “right away”
cards.noteEn: En and seguida work together as the time expression en seguida.

example.en: I will call you right away.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens right away?
cards.answerEn: Use en seguida, meaning “right away” or “immediately.”
cards.noteEn: En seguida is a fixed two-word time expression. The one-word spelling enseguida has the same meaning and is also standard.

example.en: The doctor will come right away.

cards.answerEn: right away; immediately (as part of en seguida)
cards.noteEn: In this fixed expression, seguida does not describe a feminine noun. The one-word spelling enseguida is also standard.

example.en: We will be right back.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks darse cuenta, “to realize”
cards.noteEn: Before a changed form of dar, se marks that one other person or thing—or formal usted—is the one who realizes something in the expression darse cuenta.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta del error.
example.en: She realized the mistake.

cards.promptEs: darse cuenta de (que) + hecho o situación
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone realizes or becomes aware of something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun, a form of dar, cuenta, and then de before what is realized.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun and dar must match the person: me doy cuenta, te das cuenta, se da cuenta, nos damos cuenta, and so on. Use de before a noun and de que before a full statement. Cuenta is not translated separately in this expression.

example.es: Nos dimos cuenta de que faltaba una llave.
example.en: We realized that a key was missing.

cards.answerEn: will realize (as part of se dará cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Dará is the future form of dar. With se and cuenta, it belongs to the fixed expression for realizing rather than meaning that someone will give something.

example.en: She will realize tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes darse cuenta, “to realize”
cards.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account, bill, or calculation. In darse cuenta, it is part of a fixed expression and is not translated separately.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta muy tarde.
example.en: She realized very late.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces what is realized after darse cuenta
cards.noteEn: After darse cuenta, de introduces the fact or thing that becomes clear. Before a full statement, Spanish normally uses de que.

example.es: Se dio cuenta de que era tarde.
example.en: She realized that it was late.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is right?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of tener followed by razón.
cards.noteEn: Spanish describes someone as “having reason” rather than using ser with a word for “right.” Tener changes for the person and time: tengo razón means “I am right,” and tienes razón means “you are right.” Razón stays unchanged.

example.en: Ana is right.

cards.noteEn: Devolverá is the future form used with él, ella, or formal usted.

example.en: Marta will return the book tomorrow.

cards.promptEs: el agua · el habla · del águila (nombres femeninos)
cards.questionEn: Which singular article is used immediately before a feminine noun that begins with a stressed a sound?
cards.answerEn: Use el immediately before that singular noun; use del when de + el contracts.
cards.noteEn: The noun remains feminine. Describing words still use feminine forms, and the plural uses las: el agua fría, las aguas frías. The rule applies only when the stressed a sound begins the noun.

example.es: El águila blanca voló sobre el agua fría.
example.en: The white eagle flew over the cold water.
